unmergedDoubts.whyNotMerged: All three are declarative named-policy catalogs with built-ins plus user-defined entries, so they look like one capability. Kept apart because codex's profile also carries approval granularity and an External variant, grok's carries a project-vs-global anti-hollowing merge, and cc's has no named profiles at all - it is a read/write/network axis schema. Each adds a distinct half.

codex's RestrictedToken tier is the same backend as the ih/dsh row, but codex's mechanism is the three-valued level model whose centrepiece is the Elevated tier (separate offline user, ACLs, WFP). Merging would either bury the elevated backend or imply ih and dsh have network filtering.

All three compose bubblewrap/seatbelt argv from a policy, so this was the closest call in the domain. Kept apart because grok's entire content is read-DENIAL (mode-000 bind-over, PID-suffixed placeholder, abort on a partial plan) - the only real read-deny implementation in the seven sources - and folding it into profile synthesis would hide exactly the finding this domain exists to surface.

Both are ordered allow/deny/ask ladders for tool authorization. ih's is a fixed three-layer policy whose shell boundary is an argv danger classifier; cc's is user-configurable rules drawn from eight settings sources with bypass-immune safety checks. Structurally similar, semantically not the same decision procedure.

Both let a shell command skip the ask, but the predicates differ: cc skips when the command will genuinely be sandboxed, ih skips when the danger classifier returns none. Same effect, different safety argument - and cc's second half (write-target allowlist) has no ih counterpart.

Both are fail-closed single-resolution approval paths (abort/cancel can never become allow). dsh's mechanism is a policy service with a turn-enclosed asked/decided audit pair and a signal race; cc's is handler atomicity in the UI. The overlap is real but each carries invariants the other lacks.

All three implement 'do not ask twice in a session'. codex keys a decision cache on a serialized resource-key set with subset generalisation; opencode/fork record allow RULES and re-evaluate a pending queue, and their queue has cascading reject and delete-on-exit invariants codex has no analogue for. Merged opencode+fork, left codex separate.

Adjacent (the migration rewrites the very column the persistence defines) but one is 'store the session ruleset durably, it participates in every later evaluation' and the other is an idempotent column-shape rewrite. Keeping them apart preserves that the fork's stored shape is versioned.

All three let external code set a permission outcome, and dsh/cc hooks can already emit allow. Kept apart because the fork's seam is an in-process mutable effect holder consulted before a request is created, not a subprocess hook protocol with trust hashing and timeouts.

The MDM layer is one entry in the very layer ordering the first mechanism defines, so these are two halves of one enterprise story. Kept apart because one is layer precedence plus the is_system flag and the other is a pathless source type with its own forced-read gating.

grok's documentedly user-visible effect is the always-approve lock that cc's killswitch implements, so they meet on one control. grok's is a whole managed-layer model (ordering, root-owned vs MDM authority) and cc's is a single org control whose remote half is inert in this build.

Presets bundle two independent knobs (sandbox mode and approval policy) and refuse to compose over an unconfined executor; the mode enums are a single axis. Merged grok+cc as the mode vocabulary, kept dsh's preset bundling apart because it is about how two knobs are presented and written, not about the vocabulary itself.

Both put a model in the approval path. ih's guardian can only ever restrict (allow falls through to the human, deny/timeout/malformed all deny); cc's classifier exists to WIDEN autonomy by auto-allowing. Opposite directions, so merging would misstate both.

One tree ships two rule models (V1 permission/pattern/action and V2 action/resource/effect) and the fork keeps the V1 implementation alive as a shim. I paired V1-with-shim and V2-with-V2 rather than emitting one 'permission engine' row, so the fork's in-place migration stays visible.

Three danger predicates at three different times: config-time stripping of interpreter allow-rules, path-shaped removal/glob checks, and call-time argv classification. All feed approval, none is the same check.

Same capability slot (in-process filesystem write containment) with opposite contents: dsh has a real re-canonicalising containment fence on the two mutations, ih has resolvePath '..' refusal only. A merged row would claim ih has a fence it does not have.

Both are account/server-derived gates with deliberately mixed fail postures, but one governs authentication method availability and the other governs entitlement and data-retention behaviour. Different subjects, different failure modes.
